_readme: Hand-authored overlays keyed by chapterBase id (c12_phy_ch01). Applied at build time — beats extraction where the corpus ran thin. Fields: title, subtitle, role, intro, goal, discovery{question,options,answer,hook}, mission, finale.

discovery.question: You rub a balloon on your hair and it sticks to a wall. What actually happened?
options: Electrons moved from your hair to the balloon
The balloon became magnetic
Air pressure held it against the wall
Glue molecules formed on the balloon's surface
discovery.answer: Electrons moved from your hair to the balloon
discovery.hook: Most students think rubbing 'creates' charge — it only moves it. Watch what the charges actually do.

c12_phy_ch01.mission: Make charge A positive and B negative — do the field lines reach across?
c12_phy_ch01.finale: Charge is never created or destroyed — only moved. You now know why the balloon sticks, why lightning strikes, and what Coulomb's law is really measuring.

discovery.question: Why does a bird sitting on a high-voltage wire survive unharmed?
options: No potential difference exists across its body
Its feathers insulate it
The current takes the wire instead
Birds are immune to electricity
discovery.answer: No potential difference exists across its body
discovery.hook: It is not voltage that hurts — it is voltage *difference*. That distinction is this whole chapter.

c12_phy_ch02.finale: Potential, capacitance, stored energy — you now think in terms of difference, not absolute charge. That is the mental shift this chapter demands.

discovery.question: Electrons drift at millimetres per second — yet your light turns on instantly. How?
options: The electric field pushes all electrons at once
Electrons move at light speed inside wires
Photons carry the energy, not electrons
The switch compresses electrons forward
discovery.answer: The electric field pushes all electrons at once
discovery.hook: A slow drift, an instant response — the queue moves together. That resolves the biggest confusion in current electricity.

c12_phy_ch03.mission: Close the switch — the bulb lights instantly. Now find out what the electrons were doing.
c12_phy_ch03.finale: Drift velocity, Ohm's law, resistivity — current is a coordinated march, not a sprint. Part 2 asks what happens when the wire fights back.

discovery.question: Your DNA is identical in every cell — yet a liver cell is nothing like a neuron. How?
options: Different genes are switched on in each cell type
Each cell type has different DNA sequences
Neurons lose their DNA after forming
Liver cells mutate faster
discovery.answer: Different genes are switched on in each cell type
discovery.hook: Same book, different pages read. Unzip the helix and see which pairs make it possible.

c12_bio_ch06.mission: Unzip the helix past 70% — which pairs break first?
c12_bio_ch06.finale: Replication, transcription, translation — the molecule that makes you, you. This is the chapter biology was building toward since class 6.

discovery.question: Giraffes have long necks — Lamarck said they stretched, Darwin said something else. What?
options: Long-necked giraffes survived and reproduced more
Necks grew longer each generation through use
Mutation pushed every giraffe's neck longer
Trees grew taller so giraffes adapted
discovery.answer: Long-necked giraffes survived and reproduced more
discovery.hook: Evolution does not try — it selects. That one word changes how you read this entire chapter.

c12_bio_ch07.finale: Variation, selection, drift, speciation — you now hold the framework that explains all of biology.

discovery.question: Atoms are mostly empty space — so why can't you walk through a wall?
options: Electron clouds repel each other electromagnetically
Nuclei collide head-on
Atoms are actually solid
Walls are quantum-locked
discovery.answer: Electron clouds repel each other electromagnetically
discovery.hook: Solidity is an illusion of repulsion. Rutherford's gold foil proved it a century ago.

c11_chem_ch02.mission: Place 4 electrons in the atom — which shell fills first?
c11_chem_ch02.finale: Protons, neutrons, electron clouds, orbitals — the atom stopped being a billiard ball the day you finished this.

discovery.question: A sealed bottle of soda never 'finishes' reacting — the reaction just seems to stop. What is really happening?
options: Forward and reverse reactions run at equal rates
All reactants are used up
The catalyst deactivates
Temperature drops to zero reaction
discovery.answer: Forward and reverse reactions run at equal rates
discovery.hook: Equilibrium is not stillness — it is two rivers flowing in opposite directions at exactly the same speed.

c11_chem_ch07.mission: Add more reactant — which way does the balance shift?
c11_chem_ch07.finale: Kc, Kp, Le Chatelier — you now predict which way a reaction runs before it even starts.

discovery.question: A lemon, two coins, an LED — a battery from fruit. Where does the electricity come from?
options: Electrons flow from the reactive metal through the circuit
The lemon produces electrons
The LED pushes current back
Acid stores static charge
discovery.answer: Electrons flow from the reactive metal through the circuit
discovery.hook: Every battery is a tug-of-war between two metals. The loser gives up electrons.

c12_chem_ch02.finale: Galvanic cells, electrode potentials, the Nernst equation — you now know why your phone charges and why iron rusts.

discovery.question: Draw any function without lifting your pen. What breaks at a sharp corner?
options: Differentiability — the slope jumps, so no single tangent exists
Continuity — the graph is broken
Nothing breaks, it is still a function
The function becomes undefined
discovery.answer: Differentiability — the slope jumps, so no single tangent exists
discovery.hook: Smooth versus sharp — differentiability asks whether a curve has a single slope at a point. Corners fail.

c12_math_ch05.finale: Continuity is survival; differentiability is smoothness. Every calculus result ahead of you assumes both.

discovery.question: Add up infinitely many infinitely-thin strips of area. What do you get?
options: A finite area — the definite integral
Infinity — strips add without bound
Zero — thin strips have no area
It depends on the pen thickness
discovery.answer: A finite area — the definite integral
discovery.hook: Integration is the art of making infinity finite. That paradox is the engine of all of physics.

c12_math_ch07.finale: Substitution, parts, partial fractions — you can now sum the infinite. This is the tool Newton built physics with.

discovery.question: One cone, one plane — tilt the plane and you get four different curves. How?
options: The tilt angle chooses circle, ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola
Each cone makes only one shape
The plane creates random curves
Only circles come from cones
discovery.answer: The tilt angle chooses circle, ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola
discovery.hook: Every satellite orbit and every torch beam is the same cone, sliced differently. Watch it happen.

c11_math_ch11.mission: Tilt the plane past 60° — what curve do you get?
c11_math_ch11.finale: Circle, ellipse, parabola, hyperbola — four curves, one cone, one idea. Kepler's orbits live here.

discovery.question: You can't climb the flagpole — but you can know its height from the ground. How?
options: Measure your distance and the angle up — trig does the rest
Guess from the shadow length alone
Use GPS altitude
Count the rope segments
discovery.answer: Measure your distance and the angle up — trig does the rest
discovery.hook: Trigonometry is remote measurement — ratios that let you measure what you cannot touch.

c10_math_ch08.finale: sin, cos, tan — three ratios that turn angles into distances. Surveyors, astronomers, and your phone's GPS all live here.

discovery.question: A coin lands heads 5 times in a row. What is the chance of heads on flip six?
options: Still 1/2 — the coin has no memory
Less than 1/2 — tails is 'due'
More than 1/2 — heads is 'hot'
It depends on the coin's weight
discovery.answer: Still 1/2 — the coin has no memory
discovery.hook: The gambler's fallacy has bankrupted real people. Probability does not keep score.

c10_math_ch14.finale: Sample spaces, events, odds — you now think in likelihoods, not gut feelings. That is a life skill disguised as math.

discovery.question: Ant bites burn — then soap stops the pain. What just happened on your skin?
options: A base neutralised the ant's acid
The soap cooled the skin
Ant venom evaporated
Soap blocked the nerves
discovery.answer: A base neutralised the ant's acid
discovery.hook: Acid + base → salt + water. One reaction explains ant bites, stomach acid, and soil treatment.

c10_chem_ch02.mission: Probe a pH below 4 — acid or base?
c10_chem_ch02.finale: pH, indicators, neutralisation — you can now read any liquid's chemistry by colour alone.

discovery.question: You ate a samosa an hour ago — where is it right now, doing what?
options: Being broken into molecules your cells absorb
Sitting whole in your stomach
Already converted to pure energy
Filtered out by the liver
discovery.answer: Being broken into molecules your cells absorb
discovery.hook: Digestion is disassembly — a samosa becomes glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids on an assembly line.

c10_bio_ch01.mission: Push the food to 60% — which organ is it in?
c10_bio_ch01.finale: Ingestion to egestion — your body is a processing plant. Now you know the floor plan.

discovery.question: Touch a hot pan — your hand pulls back before you even feel pain. How is that possible?
options: The spinal cord fires the response without waiting for the brain
Your hand is faster than your nerves
Pain signals travel slowly
The brain predicted the heat
discovery.answer: The spinal cord fires the response without waiting for the brain
discovery.hook: Reflexes skip the queue — that shortcut saves your hand before your brain knows why.

c10_bio_ch02.mission: Speed up the signal — how fast does the reflex fire?
c10_bio_ch02.finale: Stimulus to response in milliseconds — you traced the fastest circuit your body owns.

discovery.question: The ₹500 note in your pocket is just paper — why does a shopkeeper accept it?
options: Everyone trusts it can be exchanged for goods
The paper has intrinsic value
The RBI stores gold for every note
Law forces acceptance at gunpoint
discovery.answer: Everyone trusts it can be exchanged for goods
discovery.hook: Money is a promise we all keep together. Break the trust and paper becomes paper again.

c10_eco_ch03.finale: Barter, money, credit, banks — you now see the invisible agreement holding the whole economy up.

discovery.question: In 1919 a crowd gathered at Jallianwala Bagh. What turned a protest into a turning point?
options: The massacre showed colonial rule's true face to all of India
The crowd voted for independence that day
British apologised and left Punjab
It was the first protest in India
discovery.answer: The massacre showed colonial rule's true face to all of India
discovery.hook: Some events do not start movements — they reveal them. Scrub the timeline and watch nationalism become mass politics.

c10_hist_ch02.mission: Scrub to 80% through the era — what came before what?
c10_hist_ch02.finale: From Khilafat to Non-Cooperation to Civil Disobedience — a nation learning to say no, together.

discovery.question: Is the collection of 'all tall students' a set? Think carefully.
options: No — 'tall' is not well-defined, so membership is ambiguous
Yes — any collection is a set
Yes — if the students agree
Only if you measure them first
discovery.answer: No — 'tall' is not well-defined, so membership is ambiguous
discovery.hook: Sets demand one ruthless rule: you must always be able to say yes or no. Vagueness is not allowed in.

c11_math_ch01.finale: Well-defined, ordered, unioned, intersected — you now speak the language all of modern math is written in.

discovery.question: A 2000-year-old Indian text knew the hypotenuse rule before Pythagoras wrote it down. What makes the theorem true forever?
options: a² + b² = c² follows from the geometry itself — provable, not observed
It worked for the triangles they measured
Priests declared it sacred law
Coincidence across many examples
discovery.answer: a² + b² = c² follows from the geometry itself — provable, not observed
discovery.hook: Baudhayana stated it in the Sulba Sutras centuries before Pythagoras. Proof beats observation — that is what math is.

c8_math_ch09.finale: Legs, hypotenuse, proof — a theorem older than empires, now yours.

discovery.question: A dozen eggs, a mole of atoms — why do chemists bother with the mole at all?
options: Atoms are too small to count — the mole groups them by mass
It measures atomic weight directly
It is a unit of volume for gases
It counts electrons in a shell
discovery.answer: Atoms are too small to count — the mole groups them by mass
discovery.hook: 6.022 × 10²³ is not magic — it is the conversion factor between grams and particles.

discovery.question: Compute 103 × 97 in your head — instantly. Which identity does it?
options: No shortcut exists
discovery.hook: Identities are not formulas to memorise — they are shortcuts disguised as algebra. 103×97 just took you 3 seconds.

c9_math_ch04.finale: a²−b², (a±b)², (a±b)³ — patterns that make arithmetic collapse into instant answers.

discovery.question: You feel 'cold' touching metal and 'warm' touching wood in the same room. Same temperature — why different?
options: Metal conducts heat away from your hand faster
Wood generates its own warmth
Metal is always colder than wood
Your nerves only respond to metal
discovery.answer: Metal conducts heat away from your hand faster
discovery.hook: You never feel temperature — you feel the RATE of heat flow. That changes everything about this chapter.

discovery.question: Flip a matrix, multiply by its inverse — what do you always get back?
options: The identity matrix — ones down the diagonal
The zero matrix
The original matrix
A random matrix
discovery.answer: The identity matrix — ones down the diagonal
discovery.hook: The identity matrix is the '1' of matrix world — everything times it stays itself. That single idea solves equations in 3 unknowns.

c12_math_ch03.finale: Rows, columns, determinants — you just learned the algebra that runs every 3D game and every neural network.

discovery.question: What is the speed of a car at the *instant* the photo is taken? Not average — instant.
options: A limit — speed as the time gap shrinks to zero
Distance divided by exposure time
The speedometer reading
Zero — it was still
discovery.answer: A limit — speed as the time gap shrinks to zero
discovery.hook: Calculus was invented to answer this exact question. The limit is the trick that makes 'instant' mathematically real.

c11_math_ch13.finale: Limits, slopes, derivatives — the moment Newton cracked the code of change, you just walked through.

discovery.question: Push a box northeast while your friend pushes east — where does it actually go?
options: A single resultant direction — vectors add head-to-tail
Northeast then east alternately
The stronger push wins entirely
It spins in place
discovery.answer: A single resultant direction — vectors add head-to-tail
discovery.hook: Forces, velocities, fields — the world is made of arrows that add. This chapter teaches you to add them.

c12_math_ch10.mission: Add vector b to a — is the result just the lengths added?
c12_math_ch10.finale: Components, dot, cross — you now navigate in the language physics and game engines share.

discovery.question: Two lines can meet once, never, or everywhere — and each case has a real-world meaning. Which is which?
options: Unique / no / infinite solutions — consistent, inconsistent, dependent
All three mean no solution
Lines always meet exactly once
Parallel lines meet at infinity only in theory
discovery.answer: Unique / no / infinite solutions — consistent, inconsistent, dependent
discovery.hook: Every pair of equations is a question with three possible answers — this chapter teaches you to tell them apart instantly.

c10_math_ch03.finale: Graphical, substitution, elimination — three ways to solve the same pair. You now pick the fastest one.
